gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the BLUETTI AC180's listed 'Surge Power: 2,700W' is the same number as its Power Lifting Mode, which BLUETTI labels '(Heating Device)' and calls ideal for pure-resistive loads. For a motor load like a blender plus a mini fridge, the comparable limit is therefore the 1,800 W continuous rating, and BLUETTI publishes no separate figure above that for motor start-up.
standout_why: I compared against the cited portableenergylab.com booth page and the uncited ecoflow.com and voltandvalley.com pages. Portableenergylab defines surge vs continuous, but it names no products and has no figures for power lifting, X-Boost or cycle life. EcoFlow's blog gives DELTA 2 '2,700W burst with X-Boost' without saying X-Boost doesn't apply to motors. Volt & Valley (uncited) already says the Elite 200 V2's 3,900 W Power Lifting is resistive-only and tells readers to treat 2,600 W as the motor ceiling. None of the three pages covers the AC180, the model ChatGPT recommended, and none points out that its 'surge' and its heating-only mode share one number. So the idea is partly covered, but not for the pick.
decides: This confirms the AC180 rather than changing the pick, and it tightens the wording. The blender verdict has to rest on the 1,800 W continuous rating, not on '2,700 W surge'. A 1,500 W blender plus a running mini fridge (roughly 60–100 W) and lights leaves about 200 W of headroom under 1,800 W. If a vendor might start the blender while the fridge compressor is starting, the Elite 200 V2 (2,600 W continuous) is the safer choice. Separately, the AC180 is $499 at BLUETTI US today, not the $449 that our page and ChatGPT quoted from Nov 3.

findings.label: Surge vs Power Lifting (same number, heating-only)
findings.value: 1,800 W continuous; 'Surge Power: 2,700W'; Power Lifting Mode 2,700 W labelled '(Heating Device)'
findings.note: The spec table lists 'Surge Power: 2,700W', and the page says 'With Power Lifting Mode, it boosts output to 2700W' with the label '(Heating Device)'. Its examples are hair dryers, water heaters, electric blankets and ovens. A footnote reads '* AC180 portable power supply with outlet is ideal for pure-resistive heating devices like hair dryers, electric kettles, and heaters.' A blender is a motor load, so the comparable figure is the 1,800 W continuous rating. BLUETTI publishes no separate figure above 1,800 W for motor start-up.

findings.label: Cycle life (normalised basis)
findings.note: Rated to 80%, the same basis as the Elite 200 V2 figure below. At one market day a week (52 cycles a year), cycle life doesn't separate these candidates.

findings.label: AC recharge: headline vs spec line
findings.value: Headline '0-80% Recharging in 45Mins with 1,440W AC Input'; spec line 'AC Charging Cable: 1.3-1.8 Hours (1,440W Turbo Charging)'
findings.note: The 45-minute figure is to 80% at the 1,440 W Turbo rate. A full charge is listed as 1.3–1.8 h.

findings.label: Turbo charging is an app setting
findings.value: Turbo and silent charging modes are enabled in the BLUETTI app
findings.note: The same manual text says 'AC180 takes up to 1440W AC input and 500W DC input' and 'It also can handle a surge of 2700W.' So the manual calls it surge, while the product page restricts the 2,700 W mode to heating devices. The product page adds '*Set up this mode on BLUETTI App for a silent charging.'

findings.label: ECO mode (AC auto-off at low load)
findings.value: 'a new ECO mode that automatically turns on/off to conserve energy'
findings.note: This matters for a mini fridge whose compressor cycles off. If ECO is on, a low draw could trip the AC auto-off. The page gives no threshold, no time limit and no default state (see unsourced).
